overview.body:
**Sukunahikona** ​(*sukunahikona*) — ‌Healing, Sake, ‌Smallpox ​· Renowned ​little ​prince — ​belongs to ​the ‌Japanese tradition, ​where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Healing, ​Sake, Smallpox". ‌The ​name means ​"Renowned little ​prince"[^1].

​**Sukunahikona** is ​a tiny ‌kami ​with enormous ‌power. Floating ​to ‌Japan in ​a ‌boat of ​bark, he ‌met ​Ōkuninushi and ​helped him ‌pacify ‌and cultivate ‌the land. ​He ​taught the ‌arts ​of healing ​and sake-making, ‌and ​he became ​a protector ‌against ​smallpox and ‌illness. His ​small ​size makes ​him ​a deity ‌of the ‌overlooked ​and the ‌underestimated.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ​the name ‌as **Sukunahikona** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/sukunahikona/). The ​restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— a ‌description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*sukunahikona* survives ‌as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Japanese ​characters ​as **少彦名神**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Renowned ‌little prince"[^1].

​The ​ASCII form ‌*sukunahikona* survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Sukunahikona** recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ​detail ​of the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**s** → ​**S** ‌— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ​— Same
- ​**k** → ‌**k** ‌— Same
- ‌**u** ‌→ **u** ​— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ​**n** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ​— Same
- ​**h** ‌→ **h** ​— ​Same
- **i** ​→ ‌**i** — ​Same
- ‌**k** → ​**k** — ‌Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/sɯ.kɯ.na.hi.ko.na/** — ​Modern Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Su-** ‌— ​Voiceless alveolar ​fricative [s] ‌plus close ​back unrounded ‌[ɯ]; from ​少 'small/little'
- ‌**-ku-** — ​Voiceless velar ​stop ​[k] plus ​close back ​unrounded [ɯ]
- ‌**-na-** — ​Alveolar nasal ‌[n] plus ​open central ‌[a]
- ​**-hiko-** — ‌Voiceless glottal ​[h], close ‌front [i], ​voiceless velar ​[k], open-mid ‌[o]; from ‌彦 'prince'
- ‌**-na** ​— Alveolar ​nasal [n] ‌plus open ​central [a]

​For the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest ​approximation is: ‌'SOO-koo-nah-hee-koh-nah' ​— light, ‌even syllables; ​the final ​vowels are ​soft.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ‌the name:

- ​**Japanese** ‌— 少彦名神 ​Sukunahikona-no-kami — ​'renowned little ‌prince kami': ‌少 (suku-) ‌'small/little' + ‌彦名 (hikona) ​'renowned prince'
- ‌**Parallel ​form** — ​Sukunabikona — ​the Nihon ‌Shoki's spelling ​of the ​same name
- ​**Divine lineage** ‌— ​Son of ​Kamimusubi, one ​of the ‌three creation ​deities; companion ‌of Ōnamuchi ​(Ōkuninushi)

Sukunahikona ‌keeps its ​restoration ‌plain: plain ‌Hepburn. He ​is a ​small but ​powerful kami ​who assisted ‌Ōkuninushi in ‌shaping the ​land.

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

domains.body:
**Sukunahikona** ​is a ‌tiny ‌kami with ​enormous ​power. Floating ​to ​Japan ​in a ‌boat ​of bark, ​he ‌met Ōkuninushi ​and ‌helped him ​pacify ‌and cultivate ​the ​land. He ​taught ​the arts ​of ‌healing ​and sake-making, ‌and ​he became ‌a ​protector against ‌smallpox ​and illness. ‌His ​small size ​makes ‌him a ‌deity ‌of the ​overlooked ​and ‌the underestimated.[^1]

### ​Tiny ​Helper

The ‌Kojiki ​calls him ​a ‌kami 'small ​in ‌body'; in ​his ​bark boat ​he ​crossed the ‌sea ‌and ​became Ōnamuchi's ‌indispensable ​companion.

### Healer

​He ‌taught the ‌curing ‌of disease, ‌and ​later centuries ‌invoked ​him against ​smallpox ​and epidemic.

### ‌Sake ​God

​He taught ​the ‌brewing of ​sake, ​the offering ​that ‌mediates between ​humans ‌and kami.

### ​Land ‌Shaper

With ​Ōnamuchi ‌he pacified ‌the ​land, ​set boundaries, ​and ​made the ‌world ‌fit for ​people.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. W. G. Aston, 1896).
Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

mythology.body:
Sukunahikona's dossier is small ​but perfectly formed: the *Kojiki* (712) and the ‌*Nihon Shoki* (720) tell how a kami no ‌bigger than a child crossed the sea in ​a bark boat, partnered the great Ōkuninushi, taught ​medicine and sake, and sailed away to the ​Everlasting Land. The lesson the sources keep pressing: ​size and power are not the same thing.[^1]

### ​The Little Prince from Across the Sea (Kojiki)

‌The *Kojiki* ('Records of Ancient Matters', 712) tells ​how Ōnamuchi — the god later called Ōkuninushi, ​'Great Renowned Lord' — stood on a beach ‌in Izumo when a strange little boat came ​gliding over the sea. In it sat a ‌kami small in body, and his boat was ​woven of muku bark. Ōnamuchi asked his name, ‌and the small one answered: he was the ​son of Kamimusubi, one of the three creation ​deities, and his name was Sukunahikona, the Little ​Renowned Prince. Then came the exchange that defines ​the whole partnership: Ōnamuchi, who had struggled alone ​to make the wild land fit for people, ‌asked, in effect, whether anyone would be his ​companion in that work — and Sukunahikona answered ‌that this was why he had come. The ​meeting is the myth's thesis: the great lord ‌had strength without knowledge, and the little prince ​had knowledge without strength; the land needed both. ‌The *Nihon Shoki* ('Chronicles of Japan', 720) tells ​a parallel version with details of its own. ‌(Kojiki, trans. Philippi, 1968; Nihon Shoki, trans. Aston, ​1896.)[^2]

### Shaping the Land Together (Kojiki)

Together the ​two set about the work the *Kojiki* calls ‌making and pacifying the land. Ōnamuchi brought the ‌authority — he had survived Susanoo's trials by ‌fire and serpent and the malice of his ​eighty brothers — and Sukunahikona brought knowledge: the ​two traveled the islands fixing boundaries, subduing hostile ‌kami, and settling where rivers, rocks, and forests ​would belong to people. The *Kojiki* gives the ​partnership no single set-piece battle; its point is ‌duration — the long, unglamorous labour of turning ​wilderness into a country. When the work was ​done, the land had shrines where none had ‌been and fields where none had grown. ​Later ages read the pair as a charter ‌for Japanese rule: sovereignty as collaboration between visible ​majesty and hidden craft, the great lord above ​and the little prince below — a division ​of labour the *Kojiki* quietly credits with everything ​that made Japan habitable.

### The Physician and the ‌Brewer (Kojiki)

Before he left, Sukunahikona gave the ‌two arts for which he is still worshipped. ​The *Kojiki* credits him with teaching humanity the ‌way of healing disease and the way of ​brewing sake — medicine and wine, the twin ​consolations of the mortal condition. Sake in particular ‌became the bridge between worlds: the offering that ‌eases speech between humans and kami. His medical ‌patronage deepened in later centuries, when epidemic disease, ‌above all smallpox (*hōsō*), made his name a ​household word; the tiny prince who came in ‌a bark boat became one of the kami ​most often petitioned when illness struck, and his ​Ōsaka shrine in the old medicine quarter of ​Horie still draws those praying for health. The ‌pairing is older than any shrine: a god ​who heals and a god who brews are ​one god, because both trades turn perishable things ​— grain, herbs, time — into comfort.

### The ‌Departure for the Everlasting Land (Kojiki)

The *Kojiki* ​closes the partnership with a farewell. Sukunahikona climbed ​into his little bark boat and sailed away ​over the horizon to Tokoyo-no-kuni, the Everlasting Land ‌across the sea, the country from which he ​had come. Ōnamuchi watched him go and grieved ‌aloud: with his companion gone, how could he ​alone complete the work of the land? In ‌his loneliness he built a palace for the ​absent prince and enshrined him there, so that ‌departure became enshrinement — the myth's own explanation ‌of how a god who left Japan can ​still be worshipped in Japan. Every reading must ​face the quiet poignancy of the scene: the ​helper deities of the age of the gods ​do not stay; they equip the land and ‌withdraw, leaving mortals to carry on with what ‌they were taught. That withdrawal is the hinge ​between myth and history.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. W. G. Aston, 1896).
Chamberlain, B. H., The Kojiki: Records of Ancient Matters (1882).

syncretism.body:
Sukunahikona ​sits at ‌several crossroads ‌of Japanese ​religious ​history. In ​local tradition ​he has ​often ‌been paired ​or identified ​with Ebisu, ‌the ​laughing god ‌of fishermen ​and fortune, ‌since ​both arrive ​from across ​the sea ​and ​stand cheerfully ‌outside the ​pantheon's hierarchy; ‌shrines ​in the ‌Kansai region ​have conflated ‌the ​two. Medieval ‌*honji-suijaku* interpreters, ​mapping kami ​onto ‌buddhas, naturally ‌aligned a ‌healing deity ​with ​Yakushi, the ‌Medicine Buddha ​— an ​association ‌his later ​epidemiological cult ​made almost ‌inevitable. ​Comparativists note ‌the type: ​the tiny ​helper ​who equips ​the hero ‌is as ‌old ​as the ‌Kojiki and ​as wide ​as ‌Eurasia. But ‌his specific ‌portfolio — ‌medicine, ​sake, and ‌the conversion ​of a ​raw ​land into ‌an inhabited ​one — ​is ​distinctively Japanese, ‌and his ​partnership with ​Ōkuninushi ​anchors him ‌permanently in ​the Izumo ‌cycle.[^1]

​Kindred figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index ‌include [[asklepios|Asklēpiós]], ​[[bhaisajyaguru|Bhaiṣajyaguru]], [[brigid|Brigid]], ​[[eir|Eir]], [[gula|Gula]], ​and ​[[hygieia|Hygíeia]], each ‌linked through ‌healing / ​medicine.

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

cultural-legacy.body: Sukunahikona's ​cult ‌is still ‌alive ​where ​his story ​ended ​in ​trade. Sukunahikona ‌Jinja ​in ​the ‌Horie district ​of ‌Ōsaka ​— the ‌old ​medicine ​wholesale ​quarter — ​is ​affectionately ‌known as ​'Sukunahiko-san' ‌and ​draws prayers ‌for ​health; ‌its ​famous Fukumusume ‌mascot ​dolls ​are ceremonially ‌burned ‌each ‌New ​Year as ​scapegoat ‌figures, ​carrying away ​illness ‌with ​the flames. ​Sake ‌brewers ​have ‌claimed him ​as ​patron ​across Japan, ​and ‌pharmaceutical ‌companies invoke ​his ‌name ​in ​branding. In ‌modern ‌retellings ‌and games ‌he ​recurs ‌as ​the archetypal ​tiny-but-mighty ​spirit. ‌The afterlife ​suits ​the ​myth: a ‌deity ​who ​did ​his greatest ‌work ​as ‌a helper ​rather ‌than ​a ‌king is ‌remembered ​in ​workshops, breweries, ​and ​pharmacies ‌rather than ‌on ​thrones.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

archaeology.body: No ​excavated ‌sanctuary ‌can ​be securely ​assigned ​to ​Sukunahikona; ​his ‌presence ​is ​textual ‌and ​cultic. The ‌witnesses ​are ‌the ​manuscripts: ​the ​Kojiki ​survives ​in ‌the Shinpukuji ​manuscript ‌of ​1371–72 ‌and ​later ‌copies, ​the ‌Nihon ​Shoki in ​twelfth-century ‌and ‌later ‌codices ​— ​the ‌oldest ​stratum ​of Japanese ‌prose. ​On ​the ‌ground, ​Sukunahikona ‌Jinja ​in ​Ōsaka's Horie ​district ​preserves ‌his ‌living ​cult ‌amid ​the ​warehouses ‌of the ‌old ‌medicine ‌market, ​a ‌rare ​case ​of ​a ‌shrine and ​the ​trade ​it ‌protects ​growing ​up ​together. ‌Offerings ​of model ‌sake ​barrels ‌at ​brewing ‌shrines ‌across ​Japan ​extend ​the evidence ​from ‌paper ‌to ​practice.[^1]

meditation.body: Sukunahikona ​teaches that ‌smallness ‌is ​not weakness. ​The ​little ​prince from ​across ‌the ​sea brought ​medicine, ‌sake, ​and order ‌to ​a ‌troubled land, ​and ​he ​did it ​as ​a ‌companion rather ​than ‌a ​conqueror. He ‌is ​the ‌patron of ​those ‌whose ​power is ​underestimated ‌because ‌of their ‌size ​— ​the junior ‌partner, ​the ​assistant, the ‌craftsperson ​behind ​the throne. ‌His ​departure is ‌the ​darker ​half of ​the ​lesson: ‌helpers finish ‌the ​work ‌and leave, ​and ​the ‌credit stays ‌with ‌the ‌great. The ​Kojiki, ‌unusually, ​gives the ​grief ​to ‌the great ​one ​— ​it is ‌Ōnamuchi ​who ​mourns. To ​remember ‌Sukunahikona ​is to ‌remember ​that ‌the indispensable ​are ‌rarely ‌the celebrated, ​and ​that ​a bark ​boat ‌can ‌carry a ​civilisation.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Sukunahikona in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Sukunahikona preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Sukunahikona. The kami is honored at shrines associated with healing, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Sukunahikona gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Sukunahikona into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Sukunahikona appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, age-of-the-gods chapters (trans. Donald L. Philippi, Princeton University Press, 1968).
